title: Requirements
summary: Split functional needs from scale and drop features that do not change the design.

parts.rule: Separate functional requirements (what the system does) from non-functional ones (how well it must do it: latency, durability, consistency, cost). Write them as short bullets. Explicitly park features that do not change the architecture in this interview hour. Confirm with the interviewer before designing for a parked item. Rank the bullets so the top three drive storage and traffic choices.
parts.why: Unbounded scope is how designs become Christmas trees of boxes. A ranked list lets you cut custom domains, email receipts, or admin UIs when they do not move the storage or traffic story. Interviewers want to see you negotiate scope out loud, not silently assume an infinite product surface.
parts.example: problem: design a Dropbox-like file sync. Functional bullets: upload file, download file, list folder, create share link. Non-functional bullets: uploads durable in at least two stores, folder list p50 under 200 ms for a typical folder, conflict visible when two clients edit. Park for later: full-text search inside files, OCR on images, native offline rich editors — none of those change the core split between content-addressed blobs and a metadata database today. If the interviewer later insists on search, reopen scope and add an async index pipeline. Until then, keep the design on blob objects keyed by content hash plus a metadata DB for the folder tree. Reading the park list aloud prevents a mid-interview OCR detour that burns the remaining time.
parts.use: List requirements at the start of every system design. Revisit them when a proposed component has no matching bullet. Use the park list whenever a shiny side feature appears mid-whiteboard.
parts.refuse: Refuse treating "scale like a giant consumer app" as a requirement without numbers. Refuse building five optional products inside one hour. Refuse mixing SLAs into the functional list without naming the metric. Refuse silent multi-region assumptions when the interviewer asked for an MVP.

body:
Rule. Separate functional requirements (what the system does) from non-functional ones (how well it must do it: latency, durability, consistency, cost). Write them as short bullets. Explicitly park features that do not change the architecture in this interview hour. Confirm with the interviewer before designing for a parked item. Rank the bullets so the top three drive storage and traffic choices.

Why it matters. Unbounded scope is how designs become Christmas trees of boxes. A ranked list lets you cut custom domains, email receipts, or admin UIs when they do not move the storage or traffic story. Interviewers want to see you negotiate scope out loud, not silently assume an infinite product surface.

Worked example. problem: design a Dropbox-like file sync. Functional bullets: upload file, download file, list folder, create share link. Non-functional bullets: uploads durable in at least two stores, folder list p50 under 200 ms for a typical folder, conflict visible when two clients edit. Park for later: full-text search inside files, OCR on images, native offline rich editors — none of those change the core split between content-addressed blobs and a metadata database today. If the interviewer later insists on search, reopen scope and add an async index pipeline. Until then, keep the design on blob objects keyed by content hash plus a metadata DB for the folder tree. Reading the park list aloud prevents a mid-interview OCR detour that burns the remaining time.

[[diagram:split]]

When to use. List requirements at the start of every system design. Revisit them when a proposed component has no matching bullet. Use the park list whenever a shiny side feature appears mid-whiteboard.

When to refuse. Refuse treating "scale like a giant consumer app" as a requirement without numbers. Refuse building five optional products inside one hour. Refuse mixing SLAs into the functional list without naming the metric. Refuse silent multi-region assumptions when the interviewer asked for an MVP.
